title: Arrays and dynamic arrays
summary: Why indexing is instant, inserting is not, and how List<T> grows by doubling.

steps.title: An array is one block of memory
body: An array stores its items side by side in one block. To find `a[i]` the computer computes *start + i × itemSize* and jumps straight there: **O(1)**, no matter how long the array is.
The price is paid when you **insert in the middle**: every item after the gap has to shuffle one place to the right. Watch the boxes below as `7` and `9` slide over to make room for `5`.
The array has 4 slots but only `count = 3` are in use; the spare slot at the end is what makes the insert possible.

code: for (var i = count; i > pos; i--)

steps.prompt: Now insert `1` at the **front** of the same array. What does it print?
code: for (var i = count; i > pos; i--)
steps.explain: Inserting at the front moves **every** item: `O(n)`. Appending at the end moves none.

steps.title: Growing by doubling
body: An array cannot grow. `List<T>` hides an array inside and, when it is full, allocates one **twice as big** and copies everything across.

Copying sounds expensive, but it happens rarely. Watch the trace add 9 items: copies happen at sizes 1, 2, 4 and 8, adding up to 15 copies for 9 adds. However many items you add, the copies stay below `2n`.
So `Add` is **amortised O(1)**: the occasional slow add is paid for by all the cheap ones.

steps.prompt: The same growth rule, adding 17 items. What does it print?
steps.explain: Growth happens at 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 items: 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + 16 = 31 copies for 17 adds. Less than 2 copies per add on average.

steps.prompt: What if the list grew by a **fixed 10 slots** each time instead of doubling?
options: Adding n items would cost O(n²) copies in total
It would be faster, since less memory is wasted
Nothing changes: it is still amortised O(1)
Adding would never need to copy
steps.explain: It would copy 10, 20, 30, ... items: about `n² / 20` in total. Doubling is what keeps the average cost constant.

steps.prompt: Match each `List<int>` operation to its cost.
pairs: O(n), checks items one by one

steps.prompt: Complete `Grow`, which swaps the full array for one twice the size. `items` is the backing `int[]` field and `count` is how many of its slots are in use.
steps.explain: Only the `count` slots in use need copying. Looping to `bigger.Length` would read past the end of `items`.

steps.title: Build your own List
prompt: Write a class `IntList`, a growable list of ints backed by an array:
- `Capacity` (property): the length of the backing array. It starts at **2**.
- `void Add(int value)`: appends; when the array is full, first grow it to **twice** its length.
- `int Get(int index)`: returns the item; throws `ArgumentOutOfRangeException` when `index` is negative or `>= Count`.
- `void RemoveAt(int index)`: removes the item and shifts the later ones left (same exception rule).
starter: public int Count { get; private set; }
solution: public int Count { get; private set; }
for (var i = 0; i < Count; i++) bigger[i] = items[i];
for (var i = index; i < Count - 1; i++) items[i] = items[i + 1];
template: Dojo.Eq("a new list is empty", 0, dojoList.Count);
Dojo.Eq("two adds fit without growing", 2, dojoList.Capacity);
Dojo.Eq("the third add doubles capacity to 4", 4, dojoList.Capacity);
Dojo.Eq("a million adds are fast and correct", 999_999, dojoBig.Get(999_999));
hints: In `Add`: if `Count == items.Length`, build `new int[items.Length * 2]`, copy the first `Count` items, and swap it in. Then `items[Count] = value; Count++;`.
`RemoveAt`: check the index, then `items[i] = items[i + 1]` for `i` from `index` up to `Count - 2`, then `Count--`.
